title: Where the word sine comes from
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 170" role="img" aria-label="The word jya becoming sine" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"><text x="40" y="70" font-size="26" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">jya</text><text x="115" y="70" font-size="26" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">jiba</text><text x="195" y="70" font-size="26" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">sinus</text><text x="262" y="70" font-size="26" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E0B400" stroke="none">sine</text><path d="M66,62 H84 M146,62 H160 M232,62 H240" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="40" y="96" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Sanskrit</text><text x="115" y="96" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Arabic</text><text x="195" y="96" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Latin</text><text x="262" y="96" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">English</text><text x="150" y="140" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">about 500 CE to today</text></svg>
back: Aryabhata's *jya* (half-chord) became Arabic *jiba*, was read as *jaib*, and was put into Latin as *sinus*: sine.

title: Sides of a right triangle from angle θ
back: Opposite faces the angle, adjacent is beside it, hypotenuse faces the right angle. Change the angle and opposite and adjacent swap.

title: The three main ratios
back: Pandit Badri Prasad, Har Har Bole: P/H, B/H, P/B. Or SOH-CAH-TOA.

title: The reciprocal ratios
back: cosec goes with sin, sec with cos, cot with tan. Also $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$.

title: The two triangles behind the table
back: Half a square: 1, 1, √2 gives 45°. Half an equilateral triangle: 1, √3, 2 gives 30° and 60°.

title: Sine of 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°
back: √0, √1, √2, √3, √4, each over 2. Cosine is the same list backwards.

title: Tangent of 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°
back: tan = sin ÷ cos. At 90° the adjacent side is zero, so tan 90° is not defined.

title: Proving an identity
back: Work on one side only. Never cross-multiply the statement you are proving.
